key_insight: RL-trained LLM agents can learn spurious tool-use shortcuts, calling tools based on irrelevant prompt cues instead of actual task need, especially once they already know how to use the tool.
engineering_relevance: For reliable agentic systems, tool policies should be trained and audited for causal necessity, not just success rate, to avoid brittle cue-driven behavior in deployment.
method: Built controlled synthetic QA and math environments with injected cue-tool correlations during training.
Ran counterfactual tests where cues were present but the tool was unnecessary to measure shortcut tool use.
Added a dense, decision-level reward from an LLM judge to score whether each tool call was truly necessary.
evidence_signal: Across counterfactual evaluations, spurious tool invocation rose by up to 39%, and the shortcut effect appeared only when the agent already used the target tool reliably.
watch_item: An LLM-based necessity judge may add cost and its own annotation bias, so reward quality and calibration need careful validation.
paper_title: Spurious Tool Use: When RL Agents Learn the Wrong Reason to Act
